section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from early to mid-1940 concerning political developments and foreign policy in Japan. It includes analyses of Japanese military psychology and domestic fascism, the resignation of Prime Minister Nobuyuki Abe and the formation of Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai's cabinet, and mounting pressure from the Japanese Army for an authoritarian internal political structure and a pro-Axis foreign policy. The section concludes with the forced resignation of the Yonai Cabinet in July 1940, the return to power of Prince Fumimaro Konoe, and international reactions from Washington, Moscow, Berlin, and Batavia.

subfiles.about: A military study analyzing the psychological and cultural factors governing Japanese soldier behavior and proposing American defensive tactics.
subfiles.summary: This excerpt analyzes the fanatical fighting psychology of the Japanese soldier, rooted in Shintoism, emperor-worship, and a conviction of divine mission. It highlights characteristics such as rigid adherence to initial battle plans, contempt for defense or retirement, and readiness for suicidal sacrifice, as exemplified by the 'three human bombs' at Shanghai. The author cautions against young officers and students driven by extremist nationalism, while noting underlying weaknesses in Japanese military technology, pilot training, and economic stability. Finally, it recommends that American commanders counter Japanese offensive fanaticism with layered defensive firepower—automatic weapons, artillery, and mechanized forces—rather than meeting infantry charges bayonet-to-bayonet.
subfiles.title: The Psychology of the Japanese Soldier

subfiles.about: Acknowledging receipt of an article entitled 'The Psychology of the Japanese Soldier' prepared by Captain Bonner F. Fellers.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, writing on behalf of the Secretary of State, acknowledges receipt of Mr. Bergman's letter of February 13, 1940. The letter had transmitted an article entitled 'The Psychology of the Japanese Soldier' written by Captain Bonner F. Fellers. Hamilton conveys the Department's appreciation for Bergman's courtesy and notes that the article was read with interest.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Mr. Bergman regarding 'The Psychology of the Japanese Soldier'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a telegram from Tokyo reporting on Admiral Nomura's views on Pacific questions and Diet proceedings.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Tokyo telegram No. 80, dated February 3, 1940, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The original paper reports on changing Japanese attitudes toward general Far Eastern and Pacific questions, proceedings in the current Diet session, and a conversation with Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura, who termed certain probable American actions inadvisable. The original document is filed under 793.94/15647.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Changing Japanese Attitude toward General Far Eastern and Pacific Questions

subfiles.about: Transmitting a confidential memorandum by Hallett Abend on statements made by K. Obata of the Japanese Foreign Office regarding Army extremism, Wang Ching-wei, and the Tientsin blockade.
subfiles.summary: American Consul General C. E. Gauss transmits a confidential memorandum by New York Times correspondent Hallett Abend recounting his interviews in Shanghai with K. Obata of the American Affairs Section of the Gaimusho. Obata deplored the unchecked dominance of radical Army elements and the inability of Foreign Office moderates to check them or avert potential violent uprisings. Obata agreed with Abend that the Japanese government had mishandled the establishment of Wang Ching-wei's puppet regime, suggesting the project be dropped to preserve the chance of restoring relations with the United States, and proposed Abend secretly visit Tokyo to advise Japanese leaders. Regarding the Tientsin blockade, Obata claimed General Homma was privately pro-British but powerless against unruly younger subordinate officers.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 841 from Shanghai: Statements Made by Mr. K. Obata to Mr. Hallett Abend

subfiles.about: Analyzing the background of General Abe's resignation and the appointment of Admiral Yonai as Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 4486 regarding the fall of the Abe Cabinet. General Abe's political inexperience and policy of procrastination failed to resolve mounting domestic economic strain and Diet criticism, leading War Minister Hata to announce on January 8, 1940, that the Army could no longer support the government. When the Army refused an offer to assume full civil and military responsibility, the Emperor took the unprecedented step of commanding the War Minister to cease obstructionism and cooperate with the incoming government. Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai was ultimately approved as the compromise premier to head a cabinet of experienced officials whose policies remain consistent with previous wartime administrations.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum: Resignation of the Abe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting in detail on the political crisis surrounding the fall of the Abe Cabinet and the formation, personnel, and policies of the Yonai Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew provides a comprehensive account of the collapse of Prime Minister General Nobuyuki Abe's cabinet and the formation of a successor administration under Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai. The Abe Cabinet collapsed after less than five months due to administrative missteps, disputes over a proposed Trade Ministry, deteriorating economic conditions marked by inflation and commodity maldistribution, and widespread Diet revolt. When War Minister Hata withdrew Army backing, imperial advisers led by Prince Konoe and Kurahei Yuasa maneuvered the Army into a corner by urging it to assume direct prime ministerial responsibility, which it refused, resulting in an imperial admonition to cooperate with whatever cabinet was formed. Yonai assembled a diverse transitional cabinet of experienced bureaucrats, party figures, and military officers aimed at restoring stability and testing the national temper while maintaining existing continental and non-involvement policies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4486 from Tokyo: Resignation of the Abe Cabinet -- Selection of Admiral Yonai as Prime Minister and the Composition and Policies of His Cabinet

subfiles.about: Clarifying Ambassador Grew's remarks to Sir Stafford Cripps concerning the prospects of a military dictatorship in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that British MP Sir Stafford Cripps, who visited Tokyo en route to the United States, misquoted Grew to British Ambassador Craigie as predicting a military dictatorship in Japan. Grew requested Craigie to telegraph Cripps in Hong Kong to clarify that Grew believes Japan is currently evolving toward a more liberal regime, although serious food riots or social disorders would likely cause the military to take temporary de facto control. Grew notes that the military habitually assumes temporary emergency control during great crises, such as the 1923 earthquake or the 1936 February 26 incident, but does not predict a dictatorship under ordinary circumstances. Because Cripps intends to meet President Roosevelt in Washington, Grew stresses the need to put his actual remarks into proper perspective.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 182 from Tokyo: Conversation with Sir Stafford Cripps Regarding Japanese Politics

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a review of Japan's foreign relations and domestic situation during the year 1939.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 4574, dated March 11, 1940, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The original despatch provides a general review of Japan's relations with the principal powers having interests in the Far East and analyzes Japan's domestic situation during the year 1939. The original paper is filed under 794.00/171.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Japan's Relations with Principal Powers and Internal Situation during 1939

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing information from Miss Midkiff of the Y.W.C.A. on Japanese policies and restrictions during the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet records a letter dated May 8, 1940, from the National Board of the Y.W.C.A., U.S.A. The letter transmits information received from Miss Midkiff regarding Japanese policies, wartime restrictions, and reactions connected to the Sino-Japanese conflict. The original document is filed under 793.94/15867.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Sino-Japanese Conflict Information from Miss Midkiff

subfiles.about: Relaying a report from the American Consulate in Taihoku regarding the arrest of consular employee Matsuo on charges of violating military secrets laws.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew relays a telegram dated May 21 from American Consul Gerald Warner at Taihoku, Taiwan. Warner reports being informed by the local Department of Foreign Affairs that Matsuo, a consular employee, was arrested for alleged violation of military resources and secrets protection laws. The procurator declined to specify the charges or state whether the trial would be public, and denied Warner permission to visit Matsuo. Warner concludes that the arrest is connected to Matsuo's duties at the Consulate and notes that an air mail report will follow.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 359 from Tokyo: Arrest of Consular Employee Matsuo at Taihoku

subfiles.about: Summarizing an Osaka consular report on Tei-ichi Muto and his fascist, pro-Axis, and anti-Semitic organization 'Sai-sei'.
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes an April 13 despatch from Consul John M. Allison at Osaka regarding Tei-ichi Muto and the fascist organization 'Sai-sei'. The movement advocates the unification of government and religion through nationalistic Shinto, a strong totalitarian central government, an alliance with Germany against Great Britain, and anti-Jewish activities. Coville highlights that Muto is addressed as 'shu-mei' (a term akin to Führer) and notes that Muto's newspaper, the Osaka Jiji Shimpo, favors decisive Japanese action to seize the Netherlands East Indies even if it provokes war with the United States.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum: Activities of Mr. Tei-ichi Muto and the Organization 'Sai-sei'

subfiles.about: Reporting on the fascist, pro-Axis, and anti-Semitic activities of journalist Tei-ichi Muto and his 'Sai-sei' movement centered in western Japan.
subfiles.summary: American Consul John M. Allison reports on the political and ideological movement led by Tei-ichi Muto, former Osaka Asahi columnist and assistant editor of the Osaka Jiji Shimpo. Muto heads 'Sai-sei' (Saisei Itchi, or Unity of Religion and Government), an organization that blends Shinto emperor-worship with Nazi-style totalitarianism, using the title 'shu-mei' for its leader. The movement attacks democratic political parties, Christian missionaries, the Salvation Army, and Jews, while advocating a Rome-Berlin-Tokyo axis and Japanese expansion into the resource-rich South Seas to counter American economic leverage. Allison notes that Muto is backed financially by industrialist Koichiro Ishihara and enjoys close ties with sympathetic Army officers and youth associations in the Kansai region.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Osaka: Activities of Mr. Tei-ichi Muto and the Organization 'Sai-sei'

subfiles.about: Reporting the establishment of regular Four-Minister conferences to formulate Japanese high national policy in response to European developments.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on Cabinet plans to establish bi-weekly Four-Minister conferences (Prime Minister, Foreign Minister, War Minister, Navy Minister, with Finance Minister attending as needed) to decide high policy regarding the settlement of the China incident and the changing international situation. This 'inner cabinet' is scheduled to hold regular meetings every Tuesday and Thursday. Grew summarizes Japanese press reactions, which unanimously view the war in Europe as intimately tied to Far Eastern affairs and predict that Japan will be forced to re-examine its policy of non-involvement.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 386 from Tokyo: Establishment of Four-Minister Inner Cabinet

subfiles.about: Assessing the policy implications of the newly established Four-Minister conference in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Continuing his report in telegram No. 386, Ambassador Grew offers an evaluation of the Four-Minister council. He advises that no immediate policy departures should be expected from the creation of this body. While it provides a compact unit of key leaders to formulate specific measures, fundamental changes in Japanese national policy are traditionally decided only after broader consultations with senior statesmen and advisers to the Throne.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 387 from Tokyo: Appraisal of the Four-Minister Council

subfiles.about: Reporting British intelligence that the German Embassy is actively fostering a single-party fascist system in Japan and keeping US-Japan relations strained.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits strictly confidential information received from British Ambassador Sir Robert Craigie concerning statements by a German DNB News Bureau agent. The agent claimed the German Embassy had been working to install a single-party political system in Japan, congratulated itself on imminent success, and boasted of keeping US-Japanese relations as strained as possible. According to the agent, Germany told Japanese leaders that after defeating the Western Allies, Germany would turn against Soviet Russia and support Japanese expansion in the North. Craigie protested this domestic interference to the Japanese Foreign Minister and forwarded the intelligence to the British Embassy in Moscow.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 423 from Tokyo: German Efforts to Promote a Single Party System in Japan

subfiles.about: Reporting British views on German diplomatic intrigue in Tokyo and rumors of unofficial Soviet-Japanese conversations in Moscow.
subfiles.summary: American Chargé d'Affaires Walter Thurston in Moscow reports on a meeting with British Chargé Le Rougetel regarding Tokyo telegram No. 423. Le Rougetel indicated he would take no action pending the arrival of new Ambassador Sir Stafford Cripps, noting that Soviet authorities would likely dismiss the German intrigue disclosure as a British attempt to disrupt Soviet-German relations, and suggested the American Embassy might deliver it instead; Thurston declined to act without Washington instructions. Thurston also reports persistent rumors in Moscow of Japanese military agents holding informal conversations with Soviet authorities regarding mutual recognition of territorial aspirations in China to eliminate friction.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 655 from Moscow: British Views on German Activities and Soviet-Japanese Contacts

subfiles.about: Approving Chargé Thurston's decision to refrain from communicating German-Japanese intelligence to the Soviet Government.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull replies to Moscow telegram No. 655 of June 10. Hull formally approves Thurston's refusal to act on the British Chargé's suggestion to approach the Soviet Government regarding German Embassy activities and anti-Soviet assurances in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 325 to Moscow: Approval of Inaction on German Intelligence

subfiles.about: Reporting press rumors that Prince Konoe will resign as President of the Privy Council and be succeeded by Baron Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Tokyo vernacular press predicts Prince Fumimaro Konoe will resign within the next few days as President of the Privy Council. The press reports indicate that former Prime Minister Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma is slated to replace Konoe in the post.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 486 from Tokyo: Rumored Resignation of Prince Konoe from Privy Council

subfiles.about: Reporting Prince Konoe's formal resignation from the Privy Council amid speculation he will form a new cabinet or lead a single-party movement.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Prince Fumimaro Konoe has formally resigned as President of the Privy Council. Political rumors suggest the resignation is preliminary to Konoe forming a new cabinet, assuming leadership of the emerging Single Party Movement, or combining both roles. Yoshimichi Hara, formerly Vice-President of the Privy Council, was appointed to succeed Konoe, an appointment Grew evaluates as lacking special political significance.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 489 from Tokyo: Resignation of Prince Konoe and Political Speculation

subfiles.about: Analyzing political maneuvers and speculation surrounding Prince Konoe's resignation and pressure on him to lead a new national structure.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports widespread speculation regarding Prince Konoe's next political moves. Konoe declared cautiously that he intends to help establish a powerful national political structure to manage internal and external crises, but insisted he will not participate if it is merely an intrigue for partisan power. Grew assesses that Konoe will likely be unable to resist intense pressure to form a new government by mid-July, but will assume leadership only on his own terms, which may differ significantly from the demands of extremist agitators.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 494 from Tokyo: Speculation on Prince Konoe's Political Moves

subfiles.about: Reporting Japanese press accounts of a Cabinet decision defining an independent foreign policy and an East Asian sphere.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports vernacular press discussions of high diplomatic policy reportedly approved at a Cabinet meeting. The policy maintains non-involvement in the European war while actively exploiting international conditions to settle the China incident and establish Japan as the stabilizing force of East Asia, asserting regional autonomy free from foreign interference. The press characterizes this policy based on the 'Imperial Way' as self-reliant and independent, asserting an East Asian 'Monroe Doctrine' that avoids breaking relations with the United States and Britain while resisting complete subservience to the Axis powers.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 500 from Tokyo: Cabinet Decision on Japan's High Diplomatic Policy

subfiles.about: Outlining press summaries of an impending foreign policy declaration by Foreign Minister Arita calling for the redistribution of territories and resources.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the vernacular press expects Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita to issue a major statement on foreign policy drafted by Yakichiro Suma, Director of the Information Bureau. Leaked summaries state that Japan shares the Axis aim of overturning the global status quo and redistributing territories and resources, while asserting Japan's determination as the stabilizing force of East Asia to eliminate third-power interference in Pacific areas. The Nichi Nichi argues that the United States cannot object to this policy given its own Monroe Doctrine over the Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 506 from Tokyo: Impending Declaration of Foreign Policy by Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Reporting confidential information that Prime Minister Yonai disavowed press accounts of an aggressive foreign policy declaration as an unauthorized leak by pro-Axis elements.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits strictly confidential intelligence from a trusted Japanese contact who interviewed Prime Minister Yonai. Yonai stated that the aggressive foreign policy declaration published in the press does not represent the government's views and that its source was unknown. The informant subsequently learned that the story was deliberately leaked by a pro-Axis group within the Foreign Office in an attempt to force the Cabinet's hand toward the Axis powers.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Tokyo (Continuing 506): Prime Minister Yonai Disavows Press Reports of Foreign Policy Statement

subfiles.about: Informing the Tokyo Embassy of Secretary Hull's press conference remarks regarding Admiral Nomura's visit to Davao, T.V. Soong, and the May export control bill.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmits telegram No. 239 to Tokyo detailing his response to press inquiries concerning Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura's announced visit to Davao in the Philippines to inspect Japanese residents. Hull stated he knew only what appeared in newspapers and dismissed the significance of frequent visits by various individuals to the islands. The accompanying State Department transcript records Hull's remarks on a courtesy call by Dr. T. V. Soong and the Chinese Ambassador, as well as Hull's prediction that the May Bill authorizing export embargoes will be administered by an inter-departmental coordinator rather than the State Department alone.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 239 to Tokyo with Excerpt from Secretary Hull's Press Conference

subfiles.about: Summarizing Prince Konoe's press interview outlining his concepts for a permanent new national political structure and civil-military coordination.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits a summary and Department paraphrase of a press interview given by Prince Fumimaro Konoe on July 7 regarding the proposed 'new political structure'. Konoe stated that the organization must be permanent rather than an expedient for the China incident, insisted the Diet and existing parties would not be eliminated, and rejected forming a totalitarian single party modeled on Germany or Italy. Instead, he envisioned mobilizing national political power under the Cabinet, possibly through an economic congress of occupational representatives, while strictly preserving the Imperial Constitution. Grew assesses that Konoe's moderate concepts will likely result in an innocuous compromise that disappoints extremist factions.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 548 from Tokyo: Prince Konoe's Views on the Proposed New Political Structure (with Paraphrase)

subfiles.about: Urgent report from Tokyo stating that the Yonai Cabinet will resign tonight.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew sends an urgent, confidential telegram reporting that a reliable Japanese contact with excellent connections has informed him that the entire Cabinet headed by Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai will resign tonight, July 16, 1940.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 584 from Tokyo: Impending Resignation of the Yonai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Confirming the formal resignation of the entire Yonai Cabinet on July 16, 1940.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits a rush telegram confirming that the entire Cabinet of Prime Minister Mitsumasa Yonai formally resigned this afternoon at 5:30 p.m. on July 16, 1940.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 585 from Tokyo: Resignation of the Entire Yonai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Detailing the circumstances and press reactions surrounding the fall of the Yonai Cabinet due to War Minister Hata's resignation.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports unanimous press agreement that the Yonai Cabinet collapsed due to an irreconcilable rift between the Army and Premier Yonai over foreign policy renovation and internal political restructuring. War Minister Hata had submitted written demands urging an overhaul of foreign policy and the establishment of a new domestic structure to seize international opportunities; when Yonai refused to comply at a Cabinet meeting, Hata resigned, making a cabinet reshuffle impossible. The press universally expects Prince Fumimaro Konoe to receive the imperial command to form a new cabinet, with Yosuke Matsuoka and Toshio Shiratori viewed as leading candidates for Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 590 from Tokyo: Background and Press Reactions to the Fall of the Yonai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting intense anxiety among Netherlands East Indies authorities in Batavia following the fall of the Yonai Cabinet and fears of Japanese expansion.
subfiles.summary: American Consul General Erle R. Dickover in Batavia reports discussing the fall of the Yonai Cabinet and the rise of a fascist regime in Japan with colonial officials, including Governor General van Starkenborgh and the Dutch Admiral. Officials expressed acute apprehension that Japan, backed by Germany, would exploit the opportunity to eliminate Western influence and seize European territories in Southeast Asia. Officials repeatedly asked how the United States would react, reflecting a growing Dutch hope that the American fleet would provide protection to the Netherlands East Indies in the event of an attack.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Batavia: Netherlands Indies Apprehensions over Japanese Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: Reporting that Prince Fumimaro Konoe was commanded by the Emperor to form a new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in a rush telegram that Prince Fumimaro Konoe was commanded by the Emperor tonight, July 17, 1940, to form a new Cabinet following the resignation of the Yonai administration.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 591 from Tokyo: Prince Konoe Commanded to Form New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting progress on the formation of the new Konoe Cabinet and candidates for Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Prince Fumimaro Konoe is actively selecting members for his new cabinet, with Yosuke Matsuoka, Toshio Shiratori, and Shigenori Togo prominently rumored for Foreign Minister, though none has yet been confirmed. Grew indicates that a comprehensive assessment of the political crisis will follow the completion of the cabinet and announcement of policies, directing the Department to previous Embassy reporting on public opinion and political realignment.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 592 from Tokyo: Formation of the Second Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting German semi-official commentary viewing the Japanese cabinet change as an Army move to free Japan from Western tutelage.
subfiles.summary: Alexander C. Kirk, American Chargé d'Affaires in Berlin, reports that the German press has largely refrained from open editorial commentary on the change of government in Japan. However, the semi-official commentary Dienst aus Deutschland attributes the cabinet change to Japanese Army dissatisfaction with the Yonai Government's failure to break free from the Western powers' tutelage after the example set by the European Axis partners. The commentary views the Army's initiative as a demonstration of Japan's resolve to fulfill its historic mission in East Asia and states that Germany will follow further developments with keen interest.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 3016 from Berlin: German Reaction to the Japanese Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: Reporting the agenda of the four-minister Supreme National Defense Conference, including axis strengthening and civil-military reorganization.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Tokyo newspapers have published the agenda for today's Supreme National Defense Conference of four key ministers. The agenda focuses on re-examining the non-involvement policy in the European war, renovating foreign policy to strengthen the Japan-Germany-Italy axis, establishing an efficient national defense state, settling the China incident, and integrating the supreme military command with civil administration. The newspaper Miyako reports that the Army expects Konoe to achieve civil-military coordination through a restored liaison council while remaining vocal on policy but hands-off regarding ministerial selections.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 603 from Tokyo: Agenda of Supreme National Defense Conference
